subject: Mixed
description: Medium-difficulty practice set (20 questions) covering: Anatomy, Biochemistry, General Surgery & Orthopedics, Kinesio Therapeutics, Medicine, OBGY, Pathology & Microbiology, Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills, Physiology, Physiotherapy in Community Health, Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition, Physiotherapy in Neurosciences, Psychiatry, Psychology.

questions.question: Following moderate-intensity resistance training, what rest period is generally recommended between sets?

options.A: 10-15 seconds
options.B: 2 to 3 minutes
options.D: No rest is needed between sets

questions.explanation: For moderate-intensity resistance training, a 2- to 3-minute rest period between sets is generally recommended, with longer rest periods (>3 minutes) needed for high-intensity training of large, multi-joint muscle groups.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Rest Interval
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: Mortality statistics are described as 'virtually useless' for studying which category of disease?

options.A: Diseases with very high fatality rates
options.B: Diseases with low fatality, such as mental diseases or arthritis
options.D: Only diseases affecting children

questions.explanation: Mortality data are virtually useless for studying diseases associated with low fatality, such as mental diseases or arthritis, since these conditions rarely appear as a cause of death even though they cause significant morbidity — morbidity data are needed instead for such conditions.
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Measurement of Mortality — Limitations of Mortality Data
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: Which enzyme is most commonly used to cleave polypeptides into smaller fragments during sequence determination, due to its well-characterised cleavage specificity?

options.A: Pronase
options.B: Trypsin
options.D: Lipase

questions.explanation: Among the proteolytic enzymes with defined specificity for particular peptide bonds (trypsin, chymotrypsin, pepsin, elastase), trypsin is the most commonly used for generating predictable peptide fragments during sequence analysis.
questions.sourceBook: Satyanarayana, Biochemistry
questions.sourceChapter: Proteins and Amino Acids — Determination of Primary Structure
questions.subject: Biochemistry

questions.question: Early ambulation after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery is encouraged mainly because it:

options.A: Has no measurable benefit but is traditional practice
options.B: Reduces bladder complications and constipation, facilitates uterine drainage, and lessens the risk of puerperal venous thrombosis and embolism
options.D: Prevents postpartum haemorrhage entirely on its own

questions.explanation: Early ambulation after delivery provides a sense of well-being, reduces bladder complications and constipation, facilitates uterine drainage (hastening involution), and importantly lessens the risk of puerperal venous thrombosis and embolism.
questions.sourceBook: Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Management, Rest and Ambulation
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: Which special test is specifically associated with assessing patellofemoral (patellar) instability?

options.A: The apprehension test
options.B: McMurray test
options.D: The bounce home test

questions.explanation: The apprehension test is used to assess for patellar instability — the examiner laterally displaces the patella and observes for a look or feeling of apprehension from the patient, who fears the patella is about to dislocate.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Special Tests Commonly Performed on the Knee
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: For a diagnosis of Generalised Anxiety Disorder (GAD), the symptoms of anxiety should have persisted for at least:

options.A: 1 week
options.B: 1 month
options.D: 2 years

questions.explanation: Generalised Anxiety Disorder requires anxiety symptoms to have lasted for at least 6 months, with an insidious onset typically in the third decade and a stable, usually chronic course.
questions.sourceBook: Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry
questions.sourceChapter: Neurotic, Stress-related and Somatoform Disorders — Anxiety Disorder
questions.subject: Psychiatry

questions.question: Chronic amoebic ulcers of the colon are classically described by which shape, due to undermining of the ulcer margins by the trophozoite's lytic action?

options.A: Punched-out ulcer
options.B: Flask-shaped ulcer
options.D: Rodent ulcer

questions.explanation: Chronic amoebic ulcers are described as 'flask-shaped' because the lytic action of Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites undermines and enlarges the ulcer margins beneath a narrower surface opening, giving it a flask-like profile on cross-section.
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology
questions.sourceChapter: Infectious and Parasitic Diseases — Amoebiasis
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: 'ROWS' (Rule Out Worst-case Scenario) as a clinical strategy is best illustrated by which example?

options.A: Assuming pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness is always a pulled muscle
options.B: Actively investigating for pulmonary embolism in a patient presenting with pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness, because missing it could be fatal
options.C: Ignoring red flag symptoms in back pain to save time
options.D: Only used for patients over 65 years old

questions.explanation: ROWS forces clinicians to actively consider and rule out serious, potentially fatal diagnoses that can present with common symptoms — the classic textbook example is investigating for pulmonary embolism in a patient with pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Clinical Decision Making — Red Flags and ROWS
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: Regarding physical activity and stroke risk, which finding is reported?

options.A: Moderate to vigorous exercise is associated with about a 35% reduction in stroke risk, while light exercise (walking) does not show the same benefit
options.B: Exercise of any intensity has no effect on stroke risk whatsoever
options.C: Only vigorous exercise increases stroke risk
options.D: Light walking provides the greatest protective benefit, more than vigorous exercise

questions.explanation: Moderate to vigorous physical activity is associated with an overall 35% reduction in stroke risk, whereas light exercise such as walking alone does not appear to confer the same degree of protective benefit.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Risk Factors and Stroke Prevention
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: Although sodium's atomic weight (23) is lower than potassium's (39), Na+ moves through the resting cell membrane with greater difficulty than K+. Why?

options.A: Sodium ions carry a different electrical charge than potassium
options.B: Ions in body fluids are hydrated, and the hydrated Na+ ion is actually larger in radius than the hydrated K+ ion
options.C: Sodium is chemically unable to pass through any biological membrane
options.D: Potassium is not actually present in body fluids at rest

questions.explanation: Ions in solution are hydrated (surrounded by a shell of water molecules). Despite its lower atomic weight, hydrated Na+ has a larger effective radius than hydrated K+, which is a key reason Na+ crosses the resting membrane with more difficulty than K+.
questions.sourceBook: AK Jain, Physiology
questions.sourceChapter: The Membrane Potentials — Introduction, Size of Hydrated Ions
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.question: 'Patient-centred evidence-based medicine' is best defined as:

options.A: Applying research evidence strictly, ignoring the patient's individual circumstances and wishes
options.B: Applying best-available research evidence while taking individual patient factors (clinical and non-clinical, including values and wishes) into account
options.C: A model where patients make all treatment decisions with no clinical input
options.D: Applying guidelines only to patients under 65 years old

questions.explanation: Patient-centred evidence-based medicine combines the best available research evidence with individual patient factors — both clinical (comorbidities, prognosis) and non-clinical (social circumstances, personal values and wishes) — rather than applying guidelines mechanically to every patient.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Clinical Decision Making — Patient-Centred Evidence-Based Medicine
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: A child injured by a bicycle handlebar to the abdomen is classically at risk of injury to which structures?

options.A: The urethra and pelvis
options.B: Pancreatic, duodenal, mesenteric, or liver trauma
options.C: The small intestine or lumbar spine only
options.D: Severe crush injury to the chest exclusively

questions.explanation: Handlebar injuries classically cause focal, high-pressure blunt trauma to the upper abdomen, putting the pancreas, duodenum, mesentery, or liver at risk — distinct from lap belt injuries (small intestine/lumbar spine) or straddle injuries (urethra/pelvis).
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — Paediatric Trauma, Patterns of Injury
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: By definition, a transient ischemic attack (TIA) produces focal neurological deficits that:

options.A: Last longer than 24 hours with permanent residual damage
options.B: Do not last longer than 24 hours, with no evidence of residual brain damage afterward
options.C: Always progress to a completed stroke within 24 hours
options.D: Only ever affect vision, never motor function

questions.explanation: A TIA is a temporary interruption of blood supply producing focal neurological deficits lasting minutes to hours but, by definition, not longer than 24 hours, with no evidence of residual damage afterward. However, TIA is clinically significant as a warning sign — about 15% of strokes are preceded by a TIA, with the highest risk in the following 90 days.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Management Categories
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: Damage to Wernicke's area, located in the left temporal lobe, characteristically produces speech that is:

options.A: Completely absent — the patient cannot make any sound
options.B: Fluent in output but conveying little actual meaning, with impaired understanding of speech and written language
options.C: Slow and effortful but perfectly meaningful
options.D: Normal in every respect except pitch

questions.explanation: Wernicke's area damage markedly impairs comprehension of spoken and written language. Characteristically, the patient's own speech remains fluent in its flow and rhythm but conveys little coherent meaning.
questions.sourceBook: Morgan & King, Introduction to Psychology
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Temporal-Lobe Association Cortex, Language Functions
questions.subject: Psychology

questions.question: What key feature distinguishes an obsession from a delusion?

options.A: An obsession is recognised as irrational and ego-alien, and the patient tries to resist it; a delusion is firmly believed and not resisted
options.B: A delusion always involves washing rituals while an obsession never does
options.D: There is no meaningful difference between the two

questions.explanation: An obsession is recognised by the patient as their own thought, but perceived as foreign (ego-alien), irrational, and something they try (unsuccessfully) to resist — insight is present. A delusion, by contrast, is a fixed false belief that the patient does not recognise as irrational and does not resist, because they genuinely believe it.
questions.sourceBook: Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry
questions.sourceChapter: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder — Definitions
questions.subject: Psychiatry

questions.question: A key reason K+ efflux is not fully compensated by Na+ influx at rest (helping maintain the resting membrane potential) is that:

options.A: The resting membrane is much less permeable to Na+ than to K+
options.B: There is no Na+ present in the extracellular fluid at rest
options.C: K+ cannot actually cross the membrane at rest
options.D: Na+ and K+ have identical permeabilities at rest

questions.explanation: Because the resting membrane is much less permeable to Na+ than to K+, the modest inward leak of Na+ does not offset the outward diffusion of K+ down its concentration gradient — contributing to the net negative charge that develops inside the cell at rest.
questions.sourceBook: AK Jain, Physiology
questions.sourceChapter: The Membrane Potentials — Genesis of Resting Membrane Potential
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.question: For the vertebroscapular muscles (e.g., the rhomboids), resistance is preferably applied on the arm rather than directly on the scapula, their true point of insertion. Why?

options.A: It is simply easier for the therapist to grip the arm
options.B: The longer lever at the arm better reflects the functional demand of controlling the weight of the whole upper limb
options.C: The scapula moves too unpredictably to resist against
options.D: Resistance at the scapula risks skin breakdown

questions.explanation: Applying resistance on the arm uses a longer lever that more closely reflects the functional load these muscles must control (the weight of the arm), rather than testing at their literal anatomical insertion.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing, 9th ed.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 1: Principles of Manual Muscle Testing
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: Which drug was historically the first used effectively in the treatment of OCD, acting as a non-specific serotonin reuptake inhibitor?

options.A: Clomipramine
options.B: Haloperidol
options.D: Propranolol

questions.explanation: Clomipramine (a tricyclic antidepressant acting as a non-specific serotonin reuptake inhibitor, dosed 75-300 mg/day) was the first drug shown to be effective in OCD. SSRIs such as fluoxetine are now often preferred due to a better side-effect profile.
questions.sourceBook: Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry
questions.sourceChapter: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder — Drug Treatment
questions.subject: Psychiatry

questions.question: In the long bones of the upper limb, the 'growing ends' (which fuse with the shaft latest) are located at which joints?

options.A: Elbow joint only
options.B: Shoulder and wrist joints
options.D: All joints fuse at exactly the same time

questions.explanation: By the law of ossification, the epiphysis that appears first at a given end fuses last. In the upper limb this means the upper end of the humerus and the lower ends of both the radius and ulna are the 'growing ends' — they fuse with their shafts later than the corresponding opposite ends.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Ossification
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: A patient can clearly feel that they are touching an object (their sense of touch is intact) but cannot identify what the object is by touch alone. This deficit in recognition is called:

options.A: Anaesthesia
options.B: Agnosia
options.D: Ataxia

questions.explanation: Agnosia is a deficit in recognition despite intact basic sensation — the patient knows they are touching something but cannot identify what it is. When this occurs specifically with touch, it is called tactile agnosia, commonly seen after parietal-lobe damage.
questions.sourceBook: Morgan & King, Introduction to Psychology
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Parietal-Lobe Association Cortex
questions.subject: Psychology
